messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur was a man who had spent his life standing watch. At seventy-one, his work as a security guard was less about confrontation and more about presence, a steady figure in a crisp uniform. But for the last eight months, since the bombing at the city marathon, that presence had felt like a hollow shell. The trauma had occurred on his shift. He remembered the bright spring day, the cheerful crowds, and then the sudden, deafening roar that threw him against a barricade. In the chaos that followed, he’d been just another stunned body in a sea of screaming people, his training and his purpose vaporized in an instant of white noise and pressure.

In the aftermath, Arthur came to believe he had failed in the most fundamental way. He was the guard, the protector; that was his one important role, and he had been useless. This conviction, that a better man would have seen something or done something, became the lens through which he saw everything. It was this sense of profound inadequacy that drove him to change the small habits of his life. He could no longer sit in a diner with his wife, Joyce, unless he could secure the booth against the back wall, a position from which he could scan every person who entered. He told her it was just an old habit, but inwardly, he was certain he couldn't handle another surprise, that he was too fragile now to deal with even the slightest upset. At his part-time post guarding a quiet corporate lobby, he found himself watching people not as a professional, but with a hunter’s intensity, his eyes locking onto anyone whose hands stayed in their pockets too long, his body tensing for a threat he felt was always imminent.

This constant state of alert did strange things to his memory of the marathon. He spent hours at night, long after Joyce was asleep, replaying the event. But he wasn't trying to make sense of it; he was plotting a different outcome. He would ruminate for hours on how he might have gotten even, imagining himself tackling the young man with the backpack, being the hero he was supposed to have been. These vengeful fantasies kept the image of the bomber’s face searingly clear in his mind, a vivid and detailed portrait of malice. Yet this obsessive focus on one part of the memory left the rest of it in tatters. He couldn't form a coherent story of what had happened. There were flashes of screaming, the smell of smoke, and then long periods of numb blankness, where he recalled the events as if they had happened to a stranger on a television screen, devoid of any feeling at all.

The more he scanned rooms and re-lived his imagined revenge, the more entrenched his sense of failure became. Each time he positioned himself with his back to a wall, it was a silent admission of his own weakness, a reminder that he was no longer capable of facing the world. His hypervigilance at work, meant to prevent another failure, only served as a constant, exhausting testament to the last one. The world was dangerous, and he was the man who had proven he couldn't stop it. The rumination, which offered a brief, intoxicating hit of power, would always curdle into shame, leaving him feeling more helpless than before. This cycle had worn him down, leaving him irritable and distant. Joyce no longer suggested they go out for dinner, and his supervisor at work had gently commented on his "intensity."

It was after a particularly bad night, waking from a dream of the bomber’s face only to spend the next three hours staring at the ceiling, consumed by rage and self-loathing, that Arthur finally agreed to Joyce’s pleas to seek help. He sat in the therapist’s office, his back pressed firmly against the wall, and spoke in a low, tired voice. He wasn't sure what he hoped for, but he knew he could not continue to live as a ghost in his own life, haunted by the man he was supposed to have been.
